label: Church Hurt
framing: If the church wounded you, your pain is not a sign of weak faith. It is the wound that comes from having loved something that was supposed to be safe. Scripture never pretends God's people are clean, and the God who saw your hurt grieves the ones who caused it more than you do.
cultural: We tend to treat church hurt as a failure to forgive, hurrying the wounded toward an apology no one offered. But the Bible is unflinching about the harm done inside the household of God, and it does not ask the injured to pretend. Jesus reserved his hardest words not for the broken but for the religious who laid burdens on others and would not lift a finger. The hurt is real, and Scripture names it real.
historical: The wounds run through the whole story. The prophet Ezekiel, among the exiles after Jerusalem fell, indicted the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and the scattered sheep are still the Lord's concern. Centuries later the Donatist crisis forced Augustine, around AD 400, to wrestle with a church full of people who had failed each other badly, and he concluded the church is a field of wheat and weeds until the end, holy and wounded at once. Most of us have stood on both sides of that field. We have been hurt, and we have been the ones who hurt.
application: Do not let the people who wounded you decide whether you keep Jesus. Tell the truth about what happened, to God and to one safe person, without softening it to seem more spiritual. Take the time you need, but try not to confuse a season away to heal with a permanent exile from God's people. If what you suffered was abuse, name it as abuse, seek help, and know that staying away from the abuser is not the same as staying away from Christ.

verses.text: “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock? You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock. You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty.
verses.where: Ezekiel speaks against the shepherds of Israel, its rulers, who fed themselves while the flock went hungry, sick and scattered. God names what they failed to do, strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, search for the lost, and what they did instead: they ruled with violence and cruelty. Scripture does not treat harm done by the people charged with care as a small thing.

verses.text: I will tend My flock and make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD. I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy. I will shepherd them with justice.’
verses.where: After the charge comes a promise. God says he will shepherd his flock himself: seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak. The site's note on the chapter adds that he will judge between the strong sheep who trample the pasture and the weak, and shepherd them with justice.

verses.text: For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God.
verses.where: The psalmist could have endured an enemy's insults. What breaks him is that the attack comes from a close friend, one he walked with into the house of God. The site's plain note says a friend's betrayal hurts more than an enemy's attack, that this is true, and that the pain is not an overreaction.

verses.text: They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.
verses.where: Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples about teachers who tie heavy loads on other people's shoulders and will not lift a finger to move them. The site's note sets the picture against his own invitation, whose burden is light. Its plain note says the warning lands first on those who teach and lead in his church today.

verses.text: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”
verses.where: Jesus invites everyone worn out by their load to come to him, and calls himself gentle and humble in heart. The site's plain note says many people have heard the invitation as one more demand, and that it is spoken to anyone worn out by a kind of religion that felt like a weight they could never lift. A yoke is made for two, and the one beside you is kind.

verses.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. The hired hand is not the shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock. The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep.
verses.where: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep, and contrasts himself with the hired hand who runs when the wolf comes because he does not care for them. The site's plain note speaks to anyone hurt by shepherds who fed themselves: God condemned those shepherds, and Jesus defined a true one as a shepherd who gives his life for the sheep, not one who takes life from them. Your hurt does not mean God was like them.

verses.text: They replied, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out. When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
verses.where: A man born blind has been healed, and when he insists that the one who healed him must be from God, the authorities call him born in sin and throw him out. The site's note says they used sin as a weapon, a label for someone else. Then Jesus hears what they have done and goes to find him, and the plain note says that anyone put out by a church, a family or a town can remember that Jesus went looking for the man they threw out.

verses.text: But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.
verses.where: Jesus has just set a child among his disciples. The site's note calls this the most severe warning in the Gospels, aimed at anyone who causes a little one who believes in him to stumble, and its plain note says the words have rightly been applied to the abuse of children. The church has sometimes protected abusers and silenced children, the note says, and that is a betrayal of this very passage.

verses.text: I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock. Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them.
verses.where: Paul tells the elders of the church at Ephesus that savage wolves will come in among them, and that men from their own number will distort the truth to draw disciples after themselves. Scripture expected harm to come from inside the church, not only from outside it. The site's plain note says such people may speak from the front of a church.

verses.text: I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.
verses.where: Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first, slanders the elder, refuses to welcome traveling believers, and puts out of the church those who want to. The elder names the wrong plainly and plans to deal with it openly, without answering slander with slander. The site's plain note says the letter does not ask anyone to stay under a leader who controls, shames or harms them.

verses.text: He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.
verses.where: A hymn sets God's power over the stars beside his care for the lowly: the one who counts the stars and calls them by name heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. The site's plain note says he is not too big to notice you.

misread.taken: “Why not rather be wronged?” and the verses around it, about believers going to law before unbelievers, are used to tell someone harmed in a church not to go to the police, or to keep a crime inside the church so that it can be settled quietly.
misread.says: The site's plain note answers plainly: Paul is speaking of everyday civil disputes between believers, over money, property and business, “trivial cases” in his words, not of crimes. Nothing here tells anyone to keep a crime hidden or to settle it quietly inside the church. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul himself calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4), and Paul used the Roman courts when he needed to (Acts 25:11). His anger in this chapter is aimed at the strong who cheated the weak, not at the weak who sought help.
misread.text: The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?

whole: If someone in a church abused you, or a crime was done, or you are still in danger, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust outside that church, take a crime to the police, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Church hurt comes in more than one shape. It may have been a pastor who could not be questioned, who treated your doubts as rebellion. It may have been abuse by a leader or a volunteer, and then a second blow when the people in charge protected the one who did it. It may have been a congregation that closed ranks when you spoke, or friends who disappeared the month you divorced or fell sick. Afterward a parking lot on a Sunday morning can make you want to keep driving, and the verses that were used on you can still sound like the voice that used them.

Scripture is not surprised by any of this, and it is not neutral. Ezekiel's shepherds fed themselves and ruled the flock with violence. Jesus saved some of his sharpest words for teachers who laid heavy loads on others and would not lift a finger, and the site's note on Matthew 23 says that warning lands first on those who lead in his church today. Paul told the elders at Ephesus that wolves would rise from their own number, and the elder who wrote to Gaius named a leader who loved to be first and put faithful people out of the church. What makes church hurt cut so deep is that it comes from people who spoke for God, so the wound reaches past them toward God himself, and many who carry it are left asking whether any of it was real. When shepherds harm the flock, Scripture puts God against them, not beside them.

So the first wisdom is to tell the truth about what happened, to God and to one safe person, without softening it to sound more spiritual. The site's notes are plain: what a controlling leader or church did to you was wrong and not your fault, you are free to step away, and a crime belongs with the authorities, not only with the church. Ordinary disappointment among sinners is one thing; using God's name or a leader's place to control someone, to silence them, or to shield the one who did harm is another. Take the time you need, and do not let the people who hurt you decide whether you keep Jesus: he went looking for the man they threw out. When you are ready, a pastor or counselor outside that church can help you sort out what happened, and a church worth trusting is one where leaders can be questioned and a hurt person is believed.

The hope Scripture gives is not that the church will stop failing people. It is that God has not left his flock to the shepherds who failed it. In Ezekiel he promises to seek the lost, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak himself, and to judge between the strong sheep who trample the pasture and the weak. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and invites everyone worn out by a heavy religion to come to one who is gentle and humble in heart. The God who calls the stars by name binds up wounds, and yours are not too small for him to see.
deep.sit: What did the people who hurt you teach you to believe about God, and what does Jesus, who went looking for the man they threw out, say instead?

prayer.lead: After the shepherds who fed themselves, the psalm names the one who does not. The site's plain note says its promise is not that the sheep will never be in danger, but that the shepherd will never leave.
prayer.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.

careLines.text: If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault.
You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust.
If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities.
If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now.
A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
